messages.author: 1cd81689bd3bab9e
messages.subject: strange results for strong invariance analysis
parts:
Dear All, 

Would it be possible to help me understand the CFA results below. 

Strong invariance came out significant (0.01) and I am wanting to use the syntax below to identify some modifications. 

 mod_strong<-modificationIndices(strong)
mod_strong[mod_strong$op == "~1",]

Here's the result and I think I received no suggested modifications. Do I ignore the significance based on lack of modification indices? Or, should I conclude the intercepts are not invariant and partial invariance is not even possible due to lack of modifications?. Strangely, strict invariance was insignificant. 

> mod_strong<-modificationIndices(strong)
> mod_strong[mod_strong$op == "~1",]
 [1] lhs      op       rhs      block    group    level   
 [7] mi       epc      sepc.lv  sepc.all sepc.nox
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

I will appreciate your explanation, thank you.

parts:

Also,what you are trying to dind ou is not procided by modicication idnices, but by lavTestScore. Use the follwoing syntax, this will present a test for each parameter that equated in the model "strong", this can help you identify which items may need to release

lavTestScore(strong, univariate = TRUE)

Yes, I loaded semTools package. I am just conducting measurement invariance and here is my syntax: 

#COMPARE MODELS

Pardon me if my concern sounds trivial as I am new to all these and rocking my head against R, lavaan and SEM.

Alice.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: strange results for strong invariance analysis
parts:
Should check your session

Mauricio's right, this might have been an old bug that is already resolved.  Try installing the development version:

devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Restart R after installing, then run

library(semTools) 

Check the version is 0.5-2.911.  If you still get the error, please provide a reproducible example like Mauricio did (i.e., with some data, so I can try to track down the problem).
I will like to compare my models like the way measurementInvariance does it as described in

FYI, that article is quite problematic.  The author broke a cardinal rule of publishing about R by telling people to access a hidden function (semTools:::difftest() on p. 8, which no longer even exists).  It is also quite dated (using an old version of lavaan that still reported WRMR instead of SMR when any indicators are ordered).  Comparing models using changes in fit indices is generally a bad idea anyway: inflated Type I errors in small samples, no power to detect important problems in large samples.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29172611

I recommend taking the LRT seriously, trying to establish partial invariance, and evaluating the practical importance of any DIF you find by seeing its impact on latent parameters of interest.

https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpv020

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
